title: Meghalaya Bets Big on Lakadong Turmeric With Processing Push and Global Market Access
excerpt: From a G7 gift by PM Modi to bio-curcumin extraction plants, India's northeastern state is transforming its high-curcumin turmeric from a farm-gate crop into an export-ready brand.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Lakadong turmeric has the highest curcumin content at 7%, earning a GI tag in 2024.
  • A bio-curcumin extraction unit processes 200 kg of turmeric daily, enhancing local value chains.
  • Turmeric cultivation has expanded to 2,190 hectares, benefiting over 13,000 farmers, mostly women.
  • Meghalaya's agriculture GDP contribution has doubled from ₹5,978 crore in 2018-19 to ₹12,332 crore in 2024-25.

  • Lakadong turmeric from Meghalaya's West Jaintia Hills has the highest curcumin content of any commercially grown variety at around 7%, earning it a GI tag in 2024 and a spotlight at the G7 Summit in France.
  • A bio-curcumin extraction unit at Lashkein — the first in Northeast India — can process 200 kg of dried turmeric daily into oleoresin, powder, curcumin, and biocurcumin capsules.
  • The state has expanded turmeric cultivation to 2,190 hectares with over 20 processing units, benefiting more than 13,000 farmers, most of them women from tribal communities.
  • Agriculture's contribution to Meghalaya's gross state domestic product has more than doubled, from ₹5,978 crore in 2018-19 to ₹12,332 crore in 2024-25.

When Prime Minister Narendra Modi presented Meghalaya's Lakadong turmeric to world leaders at the G7 Summit in France in June, it was more than diplomatic showmanship. The gesture put a global spotlight on a crop that the northeastern state has spent several years transforming from a subsistence commodity into a branded, value-added export product — and the investments backing that transformation are now accelerating.

India's Highest-Curcumin Turmeric

Lakadong turmeric is grown almost exclusively in the West Jaintia Hills district of Meghalaya, where the soil and climate produce a rhizome with roughly 7% curcumin content — well above the 2-3% found in most commercially traded turmeric varieties. Curcumin is the bioactive compound prized by the global nutraceutical industry for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

The variety received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2024, formally linking its identity to its place of origin and giving it legal protection in export markets. Chief Minister Conrad K. Sangma has positioned the crop as a flagship agricultural product, and the state government's Lakadong Mission aims to scale production, processing, and branding simultaneously.

> **"Built with an investment of approximately ₹32 crore, it is designed to process over 10,000 metric tonnes of organic spices annually, including ginger, turmeric, black pepper, and chilli."**

"Built with an investment of approximately ₹32 crore, it is designed to process over 10,000 metric tonnes of organic spices annually, including ginger, turmeric, black pepper, and chilli."

From Farm Gate to Capsule

The most tangible sign of the shift is a bio-curcumin extraction unit commissioned at Lashkein block in West Jaintia Hills — the first of its kind in Northeast India. Funded by the North Eastern Council at a cost of ₹1.5 crore, the facility processes 200 kilograms of dried turmeric per day into oleoresin, curcumin powder, and biocurcumin capsules.

"The initiative is a step forward in promoting local value chains and enhancing the economic resilience of farmers in Meghalaya."

— North Eastern Council

The unit is supported by 15 Collective Marketing Centres with a combined membership of 600 farmers who supply raw and sliced turmeric. Officials say annual farmer income in the region has increased from ₹50,000 to ₹60,000 over the past two years, and more than 100 metric tonnes of raw Lakadong turmeric are processed annually into slices, powder, and oleoresin extract.

A larger facility — Northeast India's first organically certified spice processing unit — was inaugurated by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Built with an investment of approximately ₹32 crore, it is designed to process over 10,000 metric tonnes of organic spices annually, including ginger, turmeric, black pepper, and chilli. The plant holds certifications under both the National Programme for Organic Production and EU Organic Standards, opening direct access to premium international markets.

Scaling Up With PRIME Hubs

Meghalaya's broader agricultural push is anchored by the Community Public-Private Partnership model. Eight PRIME Hubs are already operational with investments exceeding ₹220 crore, processing 6,000 kg of produce daily, benefiting 15,000 farmers, and creating over 1,500 jobs. The state plans to scale the network to 55 hubs by 2032, alongside 40 large processing units and 540 micro-units.

Under the umbrella brand "Meghalaya Collectives – Organic," the state has brought together Lakadong turmeric, Khasi mandarin, Sohiong berries, and Kew pineapple under a traceable, market-ready identity. Four MoUs signed with Lulu Group Retail and other partners have established market linkages across GCC nations and major Indian cities, with organic pineapples, mandarins, and ginger already reaching Dubai's Lulu Hypermarket.

What's Next

Future of Meghalaya's Agriculture
›Plans for 55 processing hubs by 2032.
›Over 15,000 farmers benefiting from PRIME Hubs.
›Export reach expanding beyond the Middle East.

The Lakadong Mission's cultivation footprint has expanded to 2,190 hectares with support from more than 20 processing units benefiting over 13,000 farmers — the majority of them women from tribal communities who have traditionally grown the crop. The state is now pursuing additional organic certifications and expanding its export reach beyond the Middle East, with nutraceutical firms including Kerala-based Synthite Industries already sourcing Lakadong turmeric for curcumin extraction.

Agriculture's contribution to Meghalaya's gross state domestic product has more than doubled, from ₹5,978 crore in 2018-19 to ₹12,332 crore in 2024-25. For a state that has historically struggled with market access and transport infrastructure, the turmeric value chain represents a model that other northeastern states are watching closely.
